OVERVIEW.detail: Whisper transcribes, translates, and identifies speech using a Transformer sequence-to-sequence model. The whisper component handles the full audio-to-text pipeline, while normalizers standardize output text for evaluation.

explain.body: Whisper is OpenAI's general-purpose speech recognition system. Researchers and developers use it to transcribe audio into text, translate speech between languages, and identify which language is being spoken. The problem it solves: turning raw audio into accurate, readable text without needing separate models for each step of a traditional speech-processing pipeline. ![Approach](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openai/whisper/main/approach.png) The idea: a single Transformer sequence-to-sequence model is trained on many speech tasks at once. Audio is converted into a mel spectrogram (a visual frequency map of sound), encoded by a Transformer encoder, then decoded token-by-token into text. Special tokens tell the decoder which task to perform—transcribe, translate, or identify the language. `load_model()` fetches a pretrained checkpoint, `transcribe()` runs the full audio-to-text pipeline with fallback decoding strategies, and text normalizers (`BasicTextNormalizer`, `EnglishTextNormalizer`) clean the output so it can be fairly compared against reference transcripts during evaluation.

This module handles that: it keeps a registry of official checkpoints (each URL contains its own SHA256 hash), downloads only what is missing, verifies integrity, and hands back a ready-to-use `Whisper` object on whichever hardware (CPU or GPU) is available.

rows.title: Resolve checkpoint source

explain.body: When you want to transcribe speech, you need a way to start the process. This level is the front door: it lets you pick a pretrained model by name (like "base" or "large"), downloads it from Azure if it isn't already cached locally, loads the neural network weights onto your GPU or CPU, and hands you back a ready-to-use model object. It also exposes a command-line interface so you can run Whisper directly from a terminal without writing Python code. The model download URLs and known alignment heads (precomputed metadata telling which attention layers best track word timing) are stored here as dictionaries.

explain.body: Whisper processes audio in 30-second windows. This function is the orchestrator: it turns raw audio into a frequency representation (mel spectrogram), figures out what language is being spoken, then repeatedly decodes each window into text. If a decode looks wrong (too repetitive or low-confidence), it automatically retries with a higher randomness setting (`temperature`) before giving up.

rows.title: Prepare spectrogram and dtype
rows.detail: `log_mel_spectrogram` converts the audio to a mel spectrogram padded by 30 s of silence; FP16 is downgraded to FP32 on CPU.

rows.title: Auto-detect language
rows.detail: If no language is specified and the model is multilingual, `model.detect_language` runs on the first 30-second segment and picks the highest-probability language code.

rows.title: Build tokenizer and clip list
rows.detail: `get_tokenizer` is called with the resolved language and task; `clip_timestamps` is parsed into `seek_clips` pairs of frame indices.

rows.title: Define fallback decoder
rows.detail: `decode_with_fallback` tries each temperature in sequence, stopping when neither the compression-ratio nor the log-probability threshold is violated.

rows.title: Initialize sliding-window state
rows.detail: Variables `seek`, `input_stride`, `time_precision`, `all_tokens`, and `all_segments` are set up before the main decoding loop begins.

explain.body: This is what runs when you type `whisper audio.mp3` in a terminal. It reads every option from the command line, sets sensible defaults, loads the right model variant, and processes each audio file you give it — writing transcripts in the formats you asked for (plain text, SRT subtitles, JSON, etc.) and printing progress as it goes.

rows.title: Declare all arguments
rows.detail: The `argparse` parser registers every option — model, device, output format, decoding hyperparameters, and word-timestamp flags — with defaults and help strings.

rows.title: Post-process parsed values

rows.title: Validate word-timestamp options

rows.title: Transcribe each file
rows.detail: For every audio path, `transcribe` is called and the result is written via `writer`; exceptions are caught, printed, and skipped.

explain.body: When you have an audio file and want a text transcript, this is the entry point. The audio is too long to process at once, so it is sliced into 30-second chunks called segments. Each segment is converted into a mel spectrogram—a compact visual representation of sound frequencies over time. The decoder then tries to turn each spectrogram into text. If the first attempt produces garbled output (detected by high compression ratio or low probability), the system retries at a higher temperature, which adds randomness to break out of bad predictions. Temperature here means a scaling factor that controls how spread out the model's probability distribution is over possible next words. The CLI wrapper lets users run this whole pipeline from the terminal, specifying which model to load, which language to expect, and where to save results.

explain.body: Once a model is loaded, this level orchestrates the actual transcription. Audio can be long, so it is processed in 30-second sliding windows. Each window is converted into a mel spectrogram—a visual-like representation of sound frequencies over time—and fed to the model. Decoding first tries the most confident strategy (low temperature, meaning less randomness); if the output looks garbled (high compression ratio or low probability), it retries with higher temperature for diversity. This fallback loop improves reliability. After decoding, the pipeline can optionally align each word to its exact moment in the audio. Finally, it bundles all segments into a complete transcript and can write it as plain text, SRT subtitles, VTT, TSV, or JSON.

children.detail: `ModelDimensions` stores hyperparameters (layer counts, embedding sizes, attention heads) and builds the `AudioEncoder` and `TextDecoder`. `TextDecoder` stacks residual attention blocks that apply causal self-attention and cross-attention over encoder output.

children.title: Encoder Blocks
children.sub: Audio encoder with convolutions, positional embeddings, and…
children.detail: `AudioEncoder` applies two strided `Conv1d` layers followed by sinusoidal positional embeddings and a stack of `ResidualAttentionBlock` modules; custom `LayerNorm`, `Linear`, and `Conv1d` subclasses cast weights to match input dtype.

explain.body: To understand spoken audio, the model first converts the mel spectrogram (a 2-D frequency-vs-time picture of sound) into a rich set of features. Two convolution layers compress the time axis by half and extract local patterns; then a series of Transformer attention blocks let every time step look at every other, building up a full contextual representation that the text decoder will read from.

rows.title: Define dtype-safe primitives
rows.detail: `LayerNorm`, `Linear`, and `Conv1d` override `forward` / `_conv_forward` to cast weights to the input tensor's dtype, enabling mixed-precision operation.

rows.title: Compute sinusoidal positions
rows.detail: `sinusoids` generates a fixed (length × channels) matrix of interleaved sines and cosines used as positional embeddings in the encoder.

rows.title: Build multi-head attention
rows.detail: `MultiHeadAttention.qkv_attention` uses PyTorch's fused `scaled_dot_product_attention` when available, falling back to explicit scaled dot-product with optional masking.

rows.title: Stack residual blocks
rows.detail: `ResidualAttentionBlock` combines self-attention, optional cross-attention, and an MLP with layer norm and residual connections around each.

rows.title: Run audio encoder forward pass
rows.detail: `AudioEncoder.forward` applies two GELU-activated convolutions, adds the sinusoidal positional embedding, passes through all blocks, and returns `ln_post`-normalized features.

children.title: Decoder & Model
children.sub: Autoregressive text decoder and full Whisper model assembly
children.detail: `TextDecoder` embeds tokens, adds positional embeddings, runs cross-attending `ResidualAttentionBlock` layers with a causal mask, and projects back to vocabulary logits; `Whisper` wires encoder and decoder together and manages KV-cache hooks.

explain.body: The decoder is the part that actually writes words. It starts from special start tokens, then at each step looks at all previously generated tokens (but not future ones — that's the causal mask) and cross-attends to the encoder's audio features to decide which word comes next. The KV-cache avoids recomputing keys and values for tokens already seen, making generation much faster.

rows.title: Embed tokens with causal mask
rows.detail: `TextDecoder.__init__` creates token and positional embeddings and registers an upper-triangular `-inf` causal mask so each token only attends to past tokens.

rows.title: Decode to logits
rows.detail: `TextDecoder.forward` adds token and positional embeddings, runs the cross-attention blocks, layer-normalizes, then multiplies by the transposed token embedding weight to produce vocabulary logits.

rows.title: Assemble Whisper model
rows.detail: `Whisper.__init__` instantiates `AudioEncoder` and `TextDecoder` from `ModelDimensions` and registers a default alignment-heads sparse mask over the last half of decoder layers.

rows.title: Override alignment heads
rows.detail: `set_alignment_heads` base85-decodes and gzip-decompresses the packed boolean array, reshapes it to (n_layer × n_head), and registers it as a sparse buffer.

rows.title: Install KV-cache hooks
rows.detail: `install_kv_cache_hooks` registers forward hooks on every decoder key/value projection so their outputs are cached and concatenated for autoregressive reuse.

explain.body: A speech-to-text model needs two parts working together. The encoder reads the audio spectrogram and compresses it into a sequence of hidden states—numerical vectors that capture what was said. The decoder then generates text tokens one at a time, attending both to its own previously generated tokens (self-attention) and to the encoder's hidden states (cross-attention). Attention is a mechanism where the model learns which parts of one sequence are relevant to each position in another. Each attention step is wrapped in a residual block, meaning the original input is added back to the output so information flows easily through many layers. ModelDimensions is a simple data class that records how wide and deep these layers are, so the architecture can be rebuilt from a saved checkpoint.

children.sub: Selects tokens via greedy or beam search
children.detail: `detect_language` runs the encoder and reads the first token's probabilities to identify the spoken language. `TokenDecoder` defines greedy and beam-search strategies; `LogitFilter` suppresses unwanted tokens; `DecodingTask` orchestrates inference; `decode` is the public entry point.

Frozen dataclass holding temperature, beam size, task, language, suppression and timestamp options
Token decoder tracking top-K beam sequences by cumulative logprob with early stopping

children.title: Detect Language
children.sub: Identify spoken language from a mel spectrogram segment
children.detail: `detect_language` encodes the mel input, runs a single decoder forward pass with the SOT token, suppresses all non-language logits, and returns the argmax token IDs and a per-language probability dict.

explain.body: Whisper can handle 99 languages, but it needs to know which one it's hearing before it can transcribe. This function feeds a short mel spectrogram snippet through the model and asks: 'if forced to pick a language token right now, which is most likely?' The result — a ranked list of languages with probabilities — lets the transcription pipeline set itself up correctly.

rows.title: Validate tokenizer has language tokens
rows.detail: Raises `ValueError` if the tokenizer has no `language_token` in its SOT sequence, as English-only models cannot perform language ID.

rows.title: Encode audio if raw mel given
rows.detail: If the tensor is a raw mel spectrogram (not already-encoded features), `model.encoder` is called to produce audio features.

rows.title: Run single-token decoder pass
rows.detail: A batch of SOT tokens is fed to `model.logits`; the logits at position 0 (the SOT position) are extracted for language classification.

rows.title: Isolate language token logits
rows.detail: A boolean mask zeroes out all non-language token positions with `-inf`, then `argmax` and `softmax` produce token IDs and probability distributions.

rows.title: Return per-audio results
rows.detail: Single-input tensors are squeezed back to scalar/dict form; batched inputs return lists of token IDs and language-to-probability dicts.

children.title: Token Decoders
children.sub: Greedy and beam-search strategies for next-token selection
children.detail: `GreedyDecoder` picks the argmax (or samples at temperature > 0) each step; `BeamSearchDecoder` maintains `beam_size` candidate sequences, scores them cumulatively, and finalizes with patience-based early stopping.

explain.body: At each decoding step the model outputs a probability for every word-piece in its vocabulary. These classes decide which one to pick. Greedy is simple — always take the most likely — but can get stuck. Beam search keeps several parallel guesses alive at once and chooses the overall best sequence at the end, trading speed for quality.

rows.title: Define decoder interface
rows.detail: `TokenDecoder` declares the `update` and `finalize` abstract methods that both concrete decoders must implement.

rows.title: Greedy update and finalize
rows.detail: `GreedyDecoder.update` selects the highest-logit token (or samples at non-zero temperature) and accumulates log-probabilities; `finalize` pads an EOT to each sequence.

rows.title: Beam expansion step
rows.detail: `BeamSearchDecoder.update` scores all beam × vocab combinations, keeps the top `beam_size` live sequences, moves finished ones to `finished_sequences`, and calls `rearrange_kv_cache` to realign the cache.

rows.title: Beam finalization
rows.detail: `BeamSearchDecoder.finalize` tops up any beam with fewer than `beam_size` finished sequences from the remaining live candidates, then returns token lists and log-probability lists.

children.title: Logit Filters
children.sub: Suppress blank, special, and out-of-order timestamp tokens
children.detail: `SuppressBlank`, `SuppressTokens`, and `ApplyTimestampRules` each implement `LogitFilter.apply`, setting forbidden logit positions to `-inf` in-place before the decoder samples.

explain.body: Whisper outputs a mix of text tokens and special timestamp tokens. Without guardrails the model might emit blank outputs, repeat special control tokens, or produce timestamps that go backwards. These filter classes run before every sampling step and simply make illegal choices impossible by setting their logit scores to negative infinity, so the decoder never selects them.

rows.title: Define filter interface
rows.detail: `LogitFilter.apply` is the abstract method that all filters must implement, receiving mutable `logits` and the current `tokens` context.

rows.title: Suppress blank and listed tokens
rows.detail: `SuppressBlank` masks the space and EOT tokens at the very first sample position; `SuppressTokens` permanently masks a caller-supplied list of token IDs.

rows.title: Enforce timestamp pairing rules
rows.detail: `ApplyTimestampRules.apply` forces timestamps to come in pairs, forbids decreasing timestamps, suppresses non-timestamp tokens at sequence start, and caps the initial timestamp at `max_initial_timestamp_index`.

rows.title: Force timestamp when dominant
rows.detail: If the summed log-probability of all timestamp tokens exceeds the best text-token log-probability, all text token logits are set to `-inf`.

children.title: Decoding Task
children.sub: Wire inference, ranker, decoder, and filters; run the
children.detail: `DecodingTask.__init__` assembles `PyTorchInference`, `MaximumLikelihoodRanker`, a greedy or beam `TokenDecoder`, and logit filters; `_main_loop` iterates up to `sample_len` steps applying filters and the decoder.

explain.body: This class is the coordinator for a single 30-second decode. It plugs together all the pieces — the neural network forward pass, the strategy for picking tokens, the rules about which tokens are forbidden — and runs them in a loop until the model signals it is done speaking. The result is a sequence of token IDs that `transcribe` then turns into readable text.

rows.title: Assemble components
rows.detail: `__init__` validates options, then instantiates `PyTorchInference`, `MaximumLikelihoodRanker`, either `BeamSearchDecoder` or `GreedyDecoder`, and the applicable `LogitFilter` list.

rows.title: Validate option combinations
rows.detail: `_verify_options` raises `ValueError` for incompatible combinations such as `beam_size + best_of`, greedy with `best_of`, or `patience` without `beam_size`.

rows.title: Build initial token sequence
rows.detail: `_get_initial_tokens` prepends SOT sequence, optional prefix, and optional prompt tokens (truncated to fit the context window) to form the seed for decoding.

rows.title: Build suppress-token list
rows.detail: `_get_suppress_tokens` expands `-1` to the tokenizer's `non_speech_tokens`, always adds control tokens (transcribe, translate, SOT variants), and deduplicates.

rows.title: Run autoregressive decode loop
rows.detail: `_main_loop` calls `inference.logits`, reads no-speech probability on step 0, applies all logit filters, then calls `decoder.update` until EOT or context length is reached.

children.title: Decode Entry
children.sub: Public function to decode a mel spectrogram into
children.detail: `decode` normalises single/batched mel input, merges any `kwargs` into `DecodingOptions`, delegates to `DecodingTask.run`, and unwraps single results.

explain.body: This is the clean public surface that outside code (including `transcribe`) calls to turn a spectrogram into words. It hides the internal `DecodingTask` class, handles the difference between one audio clip and many, and lets callers override any decoding option by passing keyword arguments directly instead of constructing a dataclass by hand.

rows.title: Normalise input shape
rows.detail: A 2-D mel tensor (single segment) is unsqueezed to batch dimension 1 so `DecodingTask` always sees a 3-D input.

rows.title: Merge kwargs into options
rows.detail: Any extra keyword arguments are merged into the `DecodingOptions` dataclass via `replace`, allowing callers to override individual fields.

rows.title: Run and return
rows.detail: `DecodingTask(model, options).run(mel)` performs the full decode; the first element is returned for single inputs, the full list for batches.

explain.body: Once the encoder has processed audio into hidden states, the decoder must choose which text tokens to emit. Greedy decoding picks the single most likely token at every step—fast but sometimes suboptimal. Beam search keeps several candidate sequences (beams) in parallel and picks the best overall, trading speed for accuracy. Before any choice is made, logit filters intervene: they set the scores of forbidden tokens (like blank at the start, or timestamps in the wrong order) to negative infinity so those tokens can never be selected. Language detection works by feeding a short audio clip through the encoder and reading which language token the model considers most probable. DecodingTask wires all these pieces together—choosing the right decoder, applying filters, running the forward pass in a loop until an end-of-text token appears.

explain.body: This level contains the neural network itself. Whisper uses a Transformer architecture—a type of deep learning model built from layers of attention (a mechanism that lets the model focus on relevant parts of its input). The audio encoder transforms a mel spectrogram into a sequence of hidden representations capturing what was said. The text decoder then generates text tokens one at a time, attending to both the encoder output and previously generated tokens. Two decoding strategies are offered: greedy search picks the single most likely next token each step, while beam search tracks multiple candidate sequences simultaneously to find a better overall result. Language detection works by feeding a short audio clip through the encoder and checking which language token the decoder favors most.

explain.body: Before the neural network can hear anything, raw audio must be converted into a 2-D picture of frequencies over time — the mel spectrogram. This module does that conversion: it uses ffmpeg (a widely available audio tool) to read any audio format, resamples to 16 kHz mono, then applies a Short-Time Fourier Transform and a perceptually-weighted frequency scale (mel scale) to produce the grid the encoder expects.

rows.title: Define audio constants
rows.detail: Module-level constants (`SAMPLE_RATE`, `N_FFT`, `HOP_LENGTH`, `CHUNK_LENGTH`, `N_FRAMES`, etc.) fix the shared time-frequency grid used throughout the pipeline.

rows.title: Decode audio with ffmpeg
rows.detail: `load_audio` runs ffmpeg as a subprocess with `-f s16le -ac 1 -ar 16000`, captures stdout, and converts the raw bytes to a float32 numpy array normalised to ±1.

rows.title: Pad or trim to fixed length
rows.detail: `pad_or_trim` truncates or zero-pads a tensor or numpy array along a chosen axis to exactly `N_SAMPLES` (or a caller-supplied length), handling both backends.

rows.title: Load cached mel filterbank
rows.detail: `mel_filters` (LRU-cached per device) loads a pre-computed 80- or 128-band filterbank matrix from `assets/mel_filters.npz` and moves it to the target device.

rows.title: Compute log-mel spectrogram
rows.detail: `log_mel_spectrogram` runs `torch.stft` with a Hann window, squares magnitudes, multiplies by the mel filters, clamps and log10-scales, then normalizes to roughly [−1, 1].

explain.body: Before the model can process speech, raw audio must be converted into a numerical format it understands. This level handles that conversion in two steps. First, it shells out to ffmpeg—a widely-used command-line audio tool—to decode any audio format (MP3, WAV, FLAC, etc.) into a standard form: single-channel (mono) audio sampled at 16,000 times per second. Second, it applies a Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT), which breaks the audio into overlapping time windows and measures the strength of each frequency in each window. Those frequency strengths are then mapped through mel filterbanks—a set of overlapping frequency bands designed to mimic how humans perceive pitch—and converted to a logarithmic scale. The result is a mel spectrogram, essentially a 2D image of sound that the Transformer encoder can read.

children.title: Median Filter
children.sub: Smooths attention weights along the time dimension
children.detail: Applies a 1D median filter along the last tensor dimension, using a Triton CUDA kernel (`median_filter_cuda`) when on GPU or a fallback CPU sort-based path via `unfold().sort()`.

explain.body: Speech alignment needs smooth attention maps — sudden spikes would misplace word boundaries. This function slides a window along the time axis of the attention tensor and replaces each position with the middle (median) value of that window, which removes outliers without blurring edges. It runs a fast GPU kernel when available and falls back to a CPU sort trick otherwise.

rows.title: Guard short inputs
rows.detail: Returns `x` unchanged if its last dimension is too small to pad, then promotes 1D/2D tensors to 4D so `F.pad` can handle them.

rows.title: Reflect-pad the tensor
rows.detail: `F.pad` adds `filter_width // 2` mirrored values on each side of the last dimension so edge windows are well-defined.

rows.title: GPU fast path
rows.detail: On CUDA tensors, calls `median_filter_cuda` from the Triton ops module; on failure, warns and falls through to the CPU path.

rows.title: CPU fallback
rows.detail: Uses `unfold` to create sliding windows then `sort()[0][..., filter_width // 2]` to pick the median element from each window.

rows.title: Restore original rank
rows.detail: Strips the two synthetic leading dimensions added earlier so the result matches the input's original shape.

children.title: Find Alignment
children.sub: Maps text tokens to audio timestamps via attention
children.detail: Runs the Whisper model with forward hooks on cross-attention layers to collect `QKs`, normalises and median-filters them, then calls `dtw` to align token indices to frame indices and converts boundaries to `WordTiming` objects.

explain.body: To show when each word was spoken, the model's internal attention weights are captured during a forward pass — these weights reveal which audio frames the model was looking at when producing each token. Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) then finds the best monotonic path through that attention map, converting frame indices into seconds and grouping tokens into words.

rows.title: Build input token sequence
rows.detail: Prepends `sot_sequence` and `no_timestamps`, appends `eot` around the text tokens, then moves them to the model device.

rows.title: Install cross-attention hooks
rows.detail: Registers a `register_forward_hook` on every decoder block's `cross_attn` layer to capture the attention weight matrix into `QKs`.

rows.title: Forward pass and token probabilities
rows.detail: Runs the model under `torch.no_grad()` and `disable_sdpa()`, then computes per-token softmax probabilities from the sampled logits.

rows.title: Build and smooth the weight matrix
rows.detail: Stacks weights from `model.alignment_heads`, z-normalises across the time axis, then applies `median_filter` and averages across heads.

rows.title: DTW alignment
rows.detail: Calls `dtw(-matrix)` to find the least-cost path mapping token indices to time-frame indices.

rows.title: Build WordTiming list
rows.detail: Uses `tokenizer.split_to_word_tokens` and cumulative word boundaries to read start/end times and mean probabilities for each word.

children.title: Add Word Timestamps
children.sub: Attaches per-word start and end times to transcript
children.detail: Calls `find_alignment` on the full token sequence, truncates anomalously long words at sentence and segment boundaries using `median_duration`, then writes word-level timing dicts into each segment's `'words'` key.

explain.body: Transcript segments have rough start/end times from the decoder, but no per-word positions. This function takes that coarse segmentation and pins every word to an exact time range by running the alignment algorithm across all segments at once, then carefully correcting words that run implausibly long — a common artefact at pauses and sentence boundaries.

rows.title: Collect and align tokens
rows.detail: Strips special tokens from each segment, flattens them, and passes the full list to `find_alignment` to get a `WordTiming` list.

rows.title: Compute duration statistics
rows.detail: Calculates `median_duration` and `max_duration` from non-zero word durations, capping the median at 0.7 s.

rows.title: Truncate long words at sentence marks
rows.detail: Iterates the alignment and clips any word exceeding `max_duration` that falls on or after a sentence-ending punctuation character.

rows.title: Merge punctuations
rows.detail: Calls `merge_punctuations` to attach leading and trailing punctuation tokens to their adjacent words.

rows.title: Write words into segments
rows.detail: Iterates segments with their token counts as a budget, converts each `WordTiming` to a dict with `time_offset` applied, and stores them under `segment['words']`.

rows.title: Clamp boundary words to segment limits
rows.detail: After a long pause, trims the first word's start and snaps segment start/end timestamps to the first and last word's actual times.

explain.body: After transcription, you often want to know exactly when each word was spoken. The model's cross-attention weights hold this information: they show which audio frames the decoder focused on when producing each token. However, raw attention is noisy, so a median filter smooths it—replacing each value with the median of its neighbors, which removes spikes. Dynamic time warping (DTW) is an algorithm that finds the best monotonic alignment between two sequences of different lengths; here it maps tokens onto audio frames so each token gets a start and end time. Since a single word may span multiple tokens (subwords), the system groups tokens back into words and merges timing accordingly, also attaching punctuation to the preceding word rather than leaving it as a separate timed entry.

children.title: Triton Kernels
children.sub: GPU kernels for DTW and median filtering via
children.detail: Implements `dtw_kernel` as a Triton JIT kernel computing anti-diagonal DTW steps in parallel, and `median_kernel` which dynamically generates a bubble-sort Triton kernel at the requested `filter_width` via source-code rewriting.

explain.body: DTW and median filtering on large attention tensors are bottlenecks on GPU if done naively in Python. These Triton kernels run entirely on the GPU: DTW processes one anti-diagonal at a time (all independent cells in parallel), while the median kernel sorts a tiny window of values using a network sort whose code is auto-generated for the exact window size requested — avoiding any Python loop per element.

rows.title: DTW anti-diagonal kernel
rows.detail: `dtw_kernel` iterates over anti-diagonals `k`, loads three predecessor cost cells, adds the input cost, and stores the minimum plus the trace direction for each column in parallel.

rows.title: Generate median kernel source
rows.detail: `median_kernel` builds a Triton kernel string at runtime, injecting `filter_width` load statements and a full bubble-sort network as Python string replacements for the `LOAD_ALL_ROWS_HERE` and `BUBBLESORT_HERE` placeholders.

rows.title: Apply median filter on GPU
rows.detail: `median_filter_cuda` unfolds the input into sliding windows with `unfold`, retrieves the generated kernel via `median_kernel`, and launches it with one program per row of the output.

explain.body: After the model transcribes speech, you often want to know exactly when each word was spoken—for subtitles or karaoke-style highlighting. This level solves that by examining the cross-attention weights, which reveal how strongly the decoder focused on each audio frame when it produced each text token. Using Dynamic Time Warping (DTW)—an algorithm that finds the best alignment between two sequences that may move at different speeds—it maps each token to its corresponding audio moment. A median filter smooths the attention weights beforehand to reduce noise. For speed on NVIDIA GPUs, optimized Triton kernels (small programs that run directly on GPU hardware) handle both the DTW computation and the median filtering. The aligned tokens are then grouped into words with start and end times.

This module holds the authoritative list of supported languages and a reverse lookup so that common aliases like 'castilian' or 'burmese' still resolve to the right token without requiring the caller to know the ISO code.

explain.body: The decoder generates a stream of integer token ids, but downstream code needs actual words with clean boundaries. This class wraps tiktoken's byte-pair encoder, adds Whisper's task-control tokens (language, transcribe vs translate, timestamps), and provides splitting logic that handles both space-separated languages and scripts like Chinese or Japanese that have no spaces.

children.sub: Builds and caches a Whisper tiktoken encoding and
children.detail: `get_encoding` loads a `.tiktoken` vocab file, assigns incrementing ids to Whisper special tokens (language tags, timestamps, control tokens), and returns a `tiktoken.Encoding`; `get_tokenizer` selects the encoding name and defaults, then returns a cached `Tokenizer` instance.

explain.body: Whisper's vocabulary differs between its English-only and multilingual model variants, and must include hundreds of special tokens for language identification and timestamp injection that standard GPT-2 tokenizers don't have. These two cached factory functions load the right vocab file and build the full token set once per unique combination of model type, language, and task.

rows.title: Load vocabulary ranks
rows.detail: Reads the `.tiktoken` asset file for the requested encoding name, base64-decoding each token and parsing its integer rank.

rows.title: Register special tokens
rows.detail: Appends Whisper control tokens — language tags, `<|transcribe|>`, `<|nospeech|>`, and 1501 timestamp tokens — assigning sequential ids starting after the base vocabulary.

rows.title: Create tiktoken Encoding
rows.detail: Returns a `tiktoken.Encoding` with the GPT-2 regex pattern and the combined vocabulary and special token map.

rows.title: Select encoding and defaults
rows.detail: `get_tokenizer` normalises the language string via `TO_LANGUAGE_CODE`, picks `'multilingual'` or `'gpt2'` encoding, and enforces language/task defaults for multilingual mode.

explain.body: Neural language models do not read raw text—they work with tokens, which are integers representing common character sequences. Tiktoken is a fast byte-pair encoding library: it learns which pairs of bytes or characters appear most often and merges them into single tokens, building a fixed vocabulary. Whisper adds special tokens on top of this vocabulary: a start-of-transcript token, a language token (e.g. English, Japanese), and a task token (transcribe or translate). These prefixes tell the decoder what language to output and whether to translate into English. The Tokenizer class also handles splitting decoded tokens back into words for timestamp alignment, accounting for languages like Japanese and Chinese that do not use spaces between words.

explain.body: Subtitle files need each caption broken into short, timed cues — not just one block of text. This class converts the flat list of word timings produced by alignment into properly wrapped cues, keeping them within configurable character and line limits and optionally flashing each word as it is spoken (karaoke-style highlighting) by emitting a new cue every time the highlighted word changes.

rows.title: Emit plain or highlighted cues

rows.title: Write VTT and SRT files

explain.body: The CLI and API need to produce files without knowing which writer class to use. This factory centralises that dispatch: callers pass a string like `'srt'` or `'all'`, and get back a callable that accepts a result dict and writes the appropriate file — or all files at once — without any further branching in the caller.

rows.title: Return single writer

explain.body: Once transcription is done, results need to be saved in a format other tools understand. SRT and VTT are subtitle formats used by video players—they list each text segment with its start and end time so subtitles appear at the right moment. TSV is a tab-separated table suitable for spreadsheets or further processing. The writers must handle edge cases in text encoding: some terminals and files use different character sets, so make_safe ensures special characters are replaced or escaped to prevent errors. Compression ratio—how much shorter the text gets when compressed—is also computed here as a quality signal: if a transcription compresses very well, it likely contains lots of repetition, suggesting the model got stuck in a loop.

explain.body: Neural language models don't read words directly—they work with tokens, small pieces of text mapped to numbers. This level provides that mapping using tiktoken, a fast tokenizer library. It defines special tokens for tasks (transcribe vs. translate), languages, and timestamps, and knows how to split tokenized output back into words for different languages (important since languages like Japanese don't use spaces between words). Beyond tokenization, utility helpers here serve the rest of the codebase: calculating compression ratio (how repetitive text is, used to detect garbled output), formatting floating-point seconds into human-readable timestamps, safely detecting the system's text encoding, and writing final transcription results into standard subtitle and data formats.

explain.body: Whisper is an automatic speech recognition system that takes an audio file and produces a text transcript. The pipeline flows in a clear sequence: entry points let users load a pretrained model by name and start transcription from Python or the command line. Audio files are decoded and converted into mel spectrograms—compact numerical representations of sound. A Transformer encoder-decoder network processes these spectrograms, generating text tokens through greedy or beam search decoding with temperature fallback for robustness. Cross-attention weights from the decoder are then used to align each word to its precise moment in the audio via Dynamic Time Warping. Finally, a tokenizer converts between text and tokens, while utility functions format and export the transcript as plain text, SRT subtitles, VTT, or JSON.

explain.body: When comparing a transcript against a reference, punctuation and accents cause false mismatches. This module removes that noise. It first decomposes Unicode characters (e.g. turning a single accented letter into a base letter plus a combining accent mark), then discards the accent mark. Characters the decomposition cannot handle, like the German sharp-s, are mapped manually. Bracket-enclosed annotations like [laughter] are dropped entirely.

rows.title: Strip symbols and diacritics
rows.detail: `remove_symbols_and_diacritics` NFKD-decomposes the string, drops combining marks (category Mn), replaces symbols and punctuation with spaces, and substitutes `ADDITIONAL_DIACRITICS` entries.

rows.title: Strip symbols only
rows.detail: `remove_symbols` does the same replacement of mark/symbol/punctuation categories with spaces but uses NFKC so diacritics are preserved.

rows.detail: `BasicTextNormalizer.__init__` picks `remove_symbols_and_diacritics` or `remove_symbols` based on the `remove_diacritics` flag, and stores the `split_letters` option.

rows.title: Apply normalization pipeline
rows.detail: `__call__` lowercases, strips bracketed and parenthesized spans, runs the chosen cleaner, optionally splits into individual graphemes via `regex.findall`, then collapses whitespace.

children.detail: `EnglishNumberNormalizer` converts spelled-out numbers to digits; `EnglishSpellingNormalizer` chains that with diacritic removal, lowercasing, and British-to-American spelling replacement loaded from `english.json`.

explain.body: Speech-to-text transcribers often write numbers as words ("twenty three million"). To compare such output fairly against a reference that uses digits, both sides need the same form. This class converts the word form to digits by reading tokens left-to-right, recognising number-word sequences, handling sign prefixes like 'minus', currency words like 'dollars', ordinals like 'third', and decade plurals like 'twenties', and emitting the equivalent numeral.

rows.title: Build word-to-value tables
rows.detail: `__init__` populates dictionaries for `ones`, `tens`, `multipliers` and their ordinal and plural forms, plus currency symbols and sign prefixes.

rows.title: Mark literal exceptions
rows.detail: `literal_words` holds words like 'one' that should sometimes stay as words rather than be converted, preventing over-eager substitution.

rows.title: Walk token triples
rows.detail: `process_words` uses `windowed` to iterate over (prev, current, next) token triples, tracking an accumulated `value` and optional `prefix` across the window.

rows.title: Handle Arabic digits inline
rows.detail: When the current token already matches a numeric pattern, `to_fraction` parses it; if a decimal string is in progress the token is concatenated, otherwise any pending `value` is yielded first.

children.detail: `EnglishSpellingNormalizer` loads a JSON word map and replaces each token; `EnglishTextNormalizer` chains lowercasing, bracket removal, filler removal, contraction expansion, number and spelling normalization.

explain.body: Two transcripts of the same audio may differ only because one uses 'colour' and the other 'color', or one writes 'can't' and the other 'can not'. This pair of classes erases those surface differences. The spelling normalizer swaps British variants for their American equivalents word-by-word. The text normalizer orchestrates a full pipeline: lowercasing, dropping filler sounds like 'uh', expanding contractions into their full forms, standardizing numbers, standardizing spellings, and collapsing stray whitespace.

rows.title: Load spelling map
rows.detail: `EnglishSpellingNormalizer.__init__` reads `english.json` from the same directory to build a British-to-American word mapping.

rows.title: Apply word-level substitutions
rows.detail: `EnglishSpellingNormalizer.__call__` splits on spaces and replaces each word using `self.mapping.get`, leaving unknown words unchanged.

rows.title: Configure contraction replacers
rows.detail: `EnglishTextNormalizer.__init__` compiles a dict of regex patterns covering common contractions, informal speech forms, and title abbreviations, then instantiates the number and spelling normalizers.

rows.title: Run full normalization pipeline
rows.detail: `EnglishTextNormalizer.__call__` lowercases, strips brackets and fillers, expands contractions, removes punctuation while keeping numeric symbols, then calls `standardize_numbers` and `standardize_spellings` before final whitespace cleanup.

explain.body: Evaluating a speech recognizer's accuracy requires comparing its output to a known-correct transcript, but trivial differences—"twenty-one" vs. "21," "colour" vs. "color"—inflate error counts unfairly. This module tackles English-specific quirks in two layers. The first layer, number normalization, parses sequences of number words and rewrites them as digit strings using place-value arithmetic. The second layer, spelling normalization, orchestrates a full pipeline: it runs the number normalizer, strips symbols and diacritics (delegating to the basic normalizer), lowercases, and finally replaces British spellings with American ones using a bundled JSON dictionary. Together they ensure that two semantically identical English transcripts will match character-for-character.

boxes.label: Spelling Normalize
boxes.sub: Map British spellings to American and expand English

explain.body: After Whisper produces a transcript, you often need to score it against a reference—but raw text contains noise like capital letters, accents, punctuation, bracketed annotations, regional spellings, and numbers written as words. This package solves that by offering two normalizers. The basic normalizer works for any language: it strips content inside brackets, removes diacritics (accent marks on characters), drops non-letter symbols, and lowercases everything. The English normalizer builds on that foundation, adding a number normalizer that converts phrases like "three thousand four hundred" into "3400" using place-value arithmetic, and a spelling normalizer that swaps British variants ("favourite") for American ones ("favorite") via a bundled dictionary. Users import whichever normalizer fits their language and pass transcripts through it before computing word error rate.
